title: Andal
hook: an offering meant for the gods, and a jackal from the forest sniffing at it: Andal's picture of the marriage she refused

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala, told twice: a king who chooses to forget, and a king cursed to forget until a ring comes back from a fish. Did some small object hold a person for you? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

An offering is laid out for the gods. Priests have prepared it with care, by the rules, for the sacred fire. Then a jackal slips in from the forest and sniffs at it. Ruined. Nobody could offer it now. That rough little picture comes from a young woman's poem, and she's using it to describe herself. More exactly, she's describing what would happen to her if anyone so much as talked of marrying her to a man. The woman is Andal, and today she speaks for herself.
screen: `AN OFFERING FOR THE GODS.` → `A JACKAL FROM THE FOREST.` → `ANDAL SPEAKS FOR HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Year three met Andal at dawn, in the Tiruppavai, waking her friends for the dawn vow, and with the garland she tried on before her father carried it to the temple. That's the Andal of a group, singing as one cowherd girl among many. Her other work, the Nachiyar Tirumoli, the sacred words of the lady, sounds different. Here she's mostly alone, and the voice is hers. Take the jackal verse, in paraphrase. My heart is set on the Lord who holds the conch and the wheel. If anyone speaks of giving me to a mortal man, I won't live. It would be like the offering made for the gods being sniffed by a jackal of the forest. It's a startling image. She doesn't say marriage is bad. She says she is already set apart, already promised, and anything else would spoil the offering. Now notice whom she asks for help. The same book opens with her pleading with Kama, the god of desire, sweeping the ground and drawing in the sand for him, asking him to join her to the Lord. So she asks the very god of ordinary love to lead her away from an ordinary match. Two readings sit side by side. Sri Vaishnava teachers read her longing as the soul's longing for God, the way a devotee stands before the Lord. Other readers also hear a young woman saying in her own words whom she will and won't belong to. The tradition never had to pick one. It counts her among the Alvars, the poet-saints, and it keeps singing her verses.
screen: `HER OTHER BOOK, IN HER OWN VOICE` · `THE OFFERING AND THE JACKAL` · `ASKING THE GOD OF DESIRE FOR HELP` · `THE SOUL'S LONGING, A GIRL'S CHOICE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: something set apart. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing in your life that you've kept for what matters most to you. It might be an hour in the morning, a promise, a part of yourself you don't hand out to just anyone. Don't judge it. Just notice it's there, and that it's yours to keep. Breathe in, and know it's set apart. Breathe out, and let it rest. If you pray, you can offer that kept thing back to God. The bell holds the time.
Andal. The poet-saint who, in the Nachiyar Tirumoli, says she'd rather not live than be given to a man, because her heart is already the Lord's. Today's word.
Your line: Andal. Today, keep one small thing set apart for what matters most, even ten minutes, and guard it gently. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava Hindus honor Andal as one of the Alvars; her Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli are recited in temples and homes, and her shrine at Srivilliputtur is a place of pilgrimage.

fork.setup: you're Andal. your heart is set on the Lord, and you want help getting there. whom do you turn to first in the poem?
fork.reveal: she sweeps the ground, draws in the sand, and pleads with Kama to join her to the Lord: ordinary love's god, asked to lead her past an ordinary match.

trapdoor: what you thought: Andal is a name, like any other.
what it means: it's the name the tradition gave her. the story calls the girl her father found and raised Kodai.
what a scholar hears: tradition explains Andal as she who rules, the girl who won over the Lord, and the Nachiyar Tirumoli shows her doing it in her own words.
